summary.text: The defining sum satisfies \(a_{n+1}=(2^n-1)a_n+2^{\binom{n+1}{2}}\); for odd \(p\), Fermat’s theorem and \(\binom{n+2(p-1)+1}{2}-\binom{n+1}{2}=(p-1)(2n+2(p-1)+1)\) make both recurrence terms invariant modulo \(p\), while the recurrence at the initial shifted index supplies the base case, so induction gives the period. For \(p=2\), the same recurrence shows directly that every \(a_n\) with \(n\ge1\) is odd.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}2^{\binom{k+1}{2}}
       \prod_{j=k+1}^{n-1}(2^j-1),\qquad n\geq 1.
\]
Here \(\binom{k+1}{2}=k(k+1)/2\), so this is exactly the sequence in the statement. We prove that for every prime \(p\) and every \(n\geq 1\),
\[
a\bigl(n+2(p-1)\bigr)\equiv a(n)\pmod p.
\]

First derive a recurrence for \(a(n)\). In the sum defining \(a(n+1)\), separate the term with \(k=n\). Its product is empty and hence equals \(1\), so this last term is \(2^{\binom{n+1}{2}}\). For every term with \(0\leq k<n\), the product running through \(j=k+1,\ldots,n\) is obtained from the corresponding product for \(a(n)\) by adjoining the final factor \(2^n-1\). Therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(n+1)
&=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}2^{\binom{k+1}{2}}
  \left(\prod_{j=k+1}^{n-1}(2^j-1)\right)(2^n-1)
  +2^{\binom{n+1}{2}}\\
&=(2^n-1)a(n)+2^{\binom{n+1}{2}}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{1}
\]
Also, directly from the definition,
\[
a(1)=2^{\binom12}=1.
\tag{2}
\]

We now split according as \(p=2\) or \(p\) is odd.

### The prime \(p=2\)

We claim that
\[
a(n)\equiv 1\pmod 2\qquad(n\geq 1).
\tag{3}
\]
The assertion holds for \(n=1\) by (2). Suppose it holds for some \(n\geq1\). Since \(n\geq1\), we have \(2^n\equiv0\pmod2\). Moreover,
\[
\binom{n+1}{2}=\frac{n(n+1)}2>0,
\]
so \(2^{\binom{n+1}{2}}\equiv0\pmod2\). Reducing (1) modulo \(2\), we obtain
\[
a(n+1)\equiv(0-1)a(n)+0\equiv-a(n)\equiv1\pmod2,
\]
because \(-1\equiv1\pmod2\). Thus (3) follows by induction.

For \(p=2\), the proposed shift is \(2(p-1)=2\). Both \(a(n+2)\) and \(a(n)\) are congruent to \(1\) modulo \(2\), proving the desired result in this case.

### Odd primes

Now let \(p\) be an odd prime and put
\[
c=p-1.
\]
Since \(p\nmid2\), Fermat's little theorem gives
\[
2^c\equiv1\pmod p.
\tag{4}
\]
Consequently, for every nonnegative integer \(r\),
\[
2^{cr}\equiv1\pmod p,
\tag{5}
\]
and in particular
\[
2^{2c}\equiv1\pmod p.
\tag{6}
\]

We will prove by induction on \(n\geq1\) that
\[
a(n+2c)\equiv a(n)\pmod p.
\tag{7}
\]

For the base case \(n=1\), apply recurrence (1) at the index \(2c\):
\[
a(2c+1)=(2^{2c}-1)a(2c)+2^{\binom{2c+1}{2}}.
\]
The first term on the right vanishes modulo \(p\) by (6). The triangular exponent in the second term is
\[
\binom{2c+1}{2}=\frac{(2c+1)(2c)}2=c(2c+1),
\]
which is a multiple of \(c\). Hence (5) gives
\[
2^{\binom{2c+1}{2}}=2^{c(2c+1)}\equiv1\pmod p.
\]
It follows that
\[
a(1+2c)=a(2c+1)\equiv1=a(1)\pmod p,
\]
using (2). This proves (7) at \(n=1\).

For the induction step, suppose \(n\geq1\) and
\[
a(n+2c)\equiv a(n)\pmod p.
\tag{8}
\]
We compare the recurrence (1) at indices \(n+2c\) and \(n\). First, by (6),
\[
2^{n+2c}=2^n2^{2c}\equiv2^n\pmod p,
\tag{9}
\]
so the coefficients \(2^{n+2c}-1\) and \(2^n-1\) are congruent modulo \(p\).

Next compare the exponents in the inhomogeneous terms. The elementary triangular-number identity
\[
\binom{n+2c+1}{2}
=
\binom{n+1}{2}+c(2n+2c+1)
\tag{10}
\]
follows by expanding both sides: indeed,
\[
\frac{(n+2c+1)(n+2c)-n(n+1)}2
=c(2n+2c+1).
\]
The difference between the two exponents is therefore a multiple of \(c\). Using (5),
\[
\begin{aligned}
2^{\binom{n+2c+1}{2}}
&=2^{\binom{n+1}{2}}2^{c(2n+2c+1)}\\
&\equiv2^{\binom{n+1}{2}}\pmod p.
\end{aligned}
\tag{11}
\]

Now apply (1), followed by (9), the induction hypothesis (8), and (11):
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(n+2c+1)
&=(2^{n+2c}-1)a(n+2c)
  +2^{\binom{n+2c+1}{2}}\\
&\equiv(2^n-1)a(n)+2^{\binom{n+1}{2}}\\
&=a(n+1)\pmod p.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus (7) at \(n\) implies (7) at \(n+1\), completing the induction.

Since \(c=p-1\), equation (7) is precisely
\[
a\bigl(n+2(p-1)\bigr)\equiv a(n)\pmod p
\qquad(n\geq1)
\]
for every odd prime \(p\). Together with the already established case \(p=2\), this holds for every prime \(p\). Equivalently, the remainders of the two terms upon division by \(p\) are equal:
\[
a\bigl(n+2(p-1)\bigr)\bmod p=a(n)\bmod p.
\]
This proves the conjecture.
